Q315.L1t: Rounding replaces a number with a nearby value at a chosen place value, and a digit of 5 or more in the next place rounds the digit up.
Q315.L2t: Rounding to a larger place value can move the result either up or down, depending on the digits that are dropped.
Q315.L3t: Rounding 12345.6789 gives 10000 at the ten-thousands place, 12000 at the thousands, 12300 at the hundreds and 12350 at the tens. Rounding to the nearest whole number or any decimal place gives about 12346 or less, so the largest result is the one from the tens place.
Q315.L4t: The person who rounds to the nearest ten gets the highest number, so that person wins.
Q315.L2f: When you round to a given place value, the digits after that place are always kept as they are and only the digit in that place changes.
Q315.L3f: Rounding to the nearest thousand turns 12345.6789 into 13000, because any digit after the thousands place pushes the thousands digit up.
Q315.L4f: The person who rounds to the nearest thousand ends up with the highest number, so that person wins.

Q295.L1t: A truth table lists every combination of truth values for the sentence letters and computes the truth value of each premise and the conclusion in every row.
Q295.L2t: An argument is invalid if and only if at least one row of its truth table makes every premise true and the conclusion false.
Q295.L3t: A conditional is true whenever its antecedent and consequent are both true, and a conjunction is true when both conjuncts are true. So in the row where all three letters are true, both premises are true. In that row the negated first letter is false, so the conjunction in the conclusion is false.
Q295.L4t: The argument is invalid, and the row where all three letters are true is a counterexample, since it makes both premises true and the conclusion false.
Q295.L2f: A truth table for an argument with three sentence letters needs only four rows, because the third letter never changes the truth value of any premise.
Q295.L3f: In the row where the first letter is false and the other two are true, the conclusion comes out false, because a conjunction with a true negated conjunct is false.
Q295.L4f: The row where the first letter is false and the other two letters are true makes both premises true and the conclusion false, so it is a counterexample.

Q272.L1t: A curve defined by parametric equations traces out a path as the parameter varies, and calculus can be used to find quantities such as its length.
Q272.L2t: For a parametric curve, the derivatives of x and y with respect to the parameter give the velocity components along the path.
Q272.L3t: The arc length of a parametric curve is the integral over the parameter interval of the square root of the sum of the squared derivatives of x and y. Here that integrand simplifies to a constant speed, so the length is the speed times the length of the parameter interval, which covers a full period.
Q272.L4t: The length of the curve is two times pi.
Q272.L2f: The arc length of a parametric curve is the integral of the sum of the derivatives of x and y, without squaring or taking a root.
Q272.L3f: The curve covers only half of its path over the given interval, so the length is half of the full circuit.
Q272.L4f: The length of the curve is exactly the number pi, which is half of a full circuit.
